In [[Discrete geometry|discrete]] and [[computational geometry]], a set of points in the [[Euclidean plane]] or a higher-dimensional [[Euclidean space]] is said to be in '''convex position''' or '''convex independent''' if none of the points can be represented as a [[convex combination]] of the others.{{r|m02}} A [[finite set]] of points is in convex position if all of the points are [[Vertex (geometry)|vertices]] of their [[convex hull]].{{r|m02}} More generally, a [[family of sets|family]] of [[convex set]]s is said to be in convex position if they are pairwise disjoint and none of them is contained in the convex hull of the others.{{r|tv05}}

An assumption of convex position can make certain computational problems easier to solve. For instance, the [[traveling salesman problem]], NP-hard for arbitrary sets of points in the plane, is trivial for points in convex position: the optimal tour is the convex hull.{{r|dhow06}} Similarly, the [[minimum-weight triangulation]] of planar point sets is NP-hard for arbitrary point sets,<ref name="mr08"/> but solvable in [[polynomial time]] by [[dynamic programming]] for points in convex position.{{r|k80}}

The [[Erdős–Szekeres theorem]] guarantees that every set of <math>n</math> points in [[general position]] (no three in a line) in two or more dimensions has at least a logarithmic number of points in convex position.{{r|es35}} If <math>n</math> points are chosen uniformly at random in a [[unit square]], the probability that they are in convex position is{{r|v95}}
<math display=block>\left(\binom{2n-2}{n-1}/n!\right)^2.</math>

The [[McMullen problem]] asks for the maximum number <math>\nu(d)</math> such that every set of <math>\nu(d)</math> points in general position in a <math>d</math>-dimensional [[projective space]] has a [[projective transformation]] to a set in convex position. Known bounds are <math>2d+1\le\nu(d)\le 2d+\lceil(d+1)/2\rceil</math>.{{r|flvs01}}
